concept: one_line: Every tile you own has a magnet inside it whose direction only you know, and when you shove one into the shared rail the line either clamps shut or throws itself apart — the bluff is settled by physics before anybody can argue about it. | slug: kick | arm: hidden-mechanism | emotion: dread as the tile slides toward contact, then a sharp click or a visible kick that the whole table hears land | piggyback: line-pushing capture (Abalone, Shobu) with ordinary turns | audience: adults 14+ who play abstracts with a bluff in them — Abalone, Hive, Skull — and want the bluff resolved by the pieces instead of by a reveal | players 2-4, light, target_minutes 20 | fun_correct_bet: you win by arranging the rail so your opponent's only legal push detonates in your favour, which is a fact about a hidden sequence of poles you personally chose at setup. Force is irrelevant — shoving harder does nothing; the rail only obeys the polarity order. | nearest_known: Abalone (pushing a line off the board); Skull (committed hidden faces, bluff); Klask (magnets used as a toy, never as a rule).
mechanism: One printed rail 300 mm long with a sliding channel at 0.3 mm clearance, so a 5 g tile moves freely. Tiles are 24 x 18 x 10 mm with a pocket at the rim — not the centre — for one 6x3 mm N35 disc magnet, so both the pole and the direction it faces are choices. Setup: behind a printed screen each player loads seven tiles pole-out or pole-in, plus two blanks carrying a printed slug of matching mass and no magnet at all — a tile that does nothing, which is the whole bluff. Turn: push one tile into either end of the rail and let go. The line resolves itself: attracting neighbours clamp into one contiguous block, repelling neighbours open a gap, and every tile beyond that new gap is shed off the far end into the pusher's tray. Alternative turn: spend the turn testing one captured tile against one of your own behind your screen, learning its pole. Play until one hand is empty; most tiles captured wins, ties to fewest tiles still stuck in the rail.
physical_hook: Cardboard breaks: the resolution is a force between two hidden magnets acting through a wall — capture is something the rail does to itself while everyone watches, and no flat version can produce it without a table of who-repels-whom that a player has to read out and be trusted on. Molding breaks: the whole game is a rim pocket toleranced to hold a 6x3 mm disc by friction with no glue, a channel clearance tuned to 0.3 mm against a real magnet lot's pull, and blanks whose printed slug matches a magnet's mass to the gram; a mould fixes one clearance forever and cannot chase magnet strength batch to batch.
title: Kick
